quiz.question: What is the main architectural difference between a typical Linux container and a VM?
options: A container always has its own kernel
A VM has a guest kernel; a container shares the host kernel
A VM cannot have virtual memory
quiz.explanation: A virtual machine runs a complete guest operating system with its own private kernel over virtualized hardware. A container runs isolated processes that share the single host Linux kernel using namespaces and cgroups.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of a Linux namespace?
options: Isolate a process's view of system resources
quiz.explanation: Namespaces restrict what a process can see and interact with (e.g. PID namespace isolates process trees, Mount isolates filesystems, Network isolates IP addresses and routing tables). Resource limits are handled separately by cgroups.

quiz.question: Which cgroup v2 file reports the current memory charged to a cgroup?
quiz.explanation: In cgroup v2, 'memory.current' reports the total bytes of memory (anonymous, page cache, swap, kernel buffers) charged to that control group and its descendants. 'memory.max' defines the hard limit.

quiz.question: Why can a container be OOM-killed while the host still has free memory?
options: The container's effective memory limit can be reached
A VM exit always kills a process
quiz.explanation: A container is bound to its assigned cgroup resource limit (e.g. memory.max = 128MB). Even if the physical host has 16GB of unallocated RAM, reaching the cgroup limit triggers the kernel's cgroup-scoped OOM killer.

quiz.question: What is one potential benefit of huge pages?
options: They can increase TLB translation reach
They guarantee lower latency for every workload
quiz.explanation: Using 2 MiB or 1 GiB huge pages allows a fixed-size hardware TLB (e.g., 1024 entries) to cover gigabytes of address space rather than only 4 MiB, drastically reducing expensive multi-level page table walks.

quiz.question: What is the primary performance concern in NUMA systems?
options: Every memory access has identical latency
Memory locality can affect access latency and bandwidth
quiz.explanation: In Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA) multi-socket systems, accessing memory attached to the local CPU socket is fast, whereas accessing remote node memory across the interconnect bus incurs 2x to 3x higher latency and reduced bandwidth.

theorySections.title: Memory-Mapped I/O and Shared Memory
paragraphs: MMIO vs File Mappings · mmap Flags · Synchronization · SIGBUS Safety

Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO) allows the CPU to communicate with hardware device registers using standard memory instructions (MOV, load, store) rather than dedicated I/O port instructions (IN/ OUT). The OS and CPU configure these memory regions with special caching attributes (e.g. Uncacheable) to ensure writes reach the device immediately without CPU cache reordering.

Writes to memory are visible to other processes mapping the same object and are flushed back to the underlying storage file. Requires process-shared mutexes or atomic operations for race-free updates.
Creates a Copy-On-Write (COW) mapping. Reads access the underlying file directly; modifications create a private anonymous frame invisible to other processes and never written back to disk.
Memory is not backed by any filesystem file (fd = -1). Used by memory allocators (malloc) for heap regions and zero-filled pages on demand.

theorySections.title: Huge Pages, NUMA and Memory Locality
paragraphs: TLB Reach · 2MB / 1GB Pages · Non-Uniform Memory Access · First-Touch Allocation
Modern x86-64 processors default to 4 KiB pages. For massive in-memory databases (PostgreSQL, Redis) and virtualization hypervisors, 4 KiB pages create a severe performance bottleneck:

In multi-socket servers, memory is partitioned into NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) nodes. Each CPU socket has high-speed direct access to its local RAM channels, but accessing RAM attached to another socket over the interconnect bus (Intel UPI / AMD Infinity Fabric) incurs a 2x to 3x latency penalty.

When malloc() is called, Linux allocates virtual address space only. Physical memory is not mapped until the first thread touches (writes to) the page. By default, Linux allocates the physical frame on the NUMA node where the faulting thread is currently scheduled!
Use numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./app to pin threads and memory allocations to the same socket, eliminating cross-socket interconnect thrashing.

Hardware virtualization (Intel VT-x / AMD-V) introduces new CPU operational modes: VMX Root Operation (where the hypervisor executes with full hardware control) and VMX Non-Root Operation (where the guest OS executes with sensitive instructions trapped).

Runs as an application inside a host operating system (e.g. VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Subject to host OS scheduling latency, buffer double-caching, and context-switch overhead.
